summary: This document summarizes a workshop on Smart Object Security held in Paris on 23 March 2012. Participants shared thoughts on using existing and widely deployed security mechanisms for smart objects, and the report lists conclusions and recommendations for the IETF.

eli5.summary: Tiny connected gadgets also need to be safe. This RFC is a summary of what a group of experts discussed at a meeting about that and what they suggested.

subtitle: What experts learned about securing tiny internet-connected devices

tldr.problem: Internet of Things devices have tight constraints on memory, power and bandwidth, making it unclear how to apply standard security mechanisms without compromising their operation.
tldr.mechanism: A 2012 workshop brought together security experts to share implementation experiences and discuss how existing IETF security protocols could be customized and optimized for constrained smart objects.
tldr.outcome: Participants concluded that existing IETF protocols like TLS and DTLS are viable for smart objects with careful optimization, but security architecture cannot be one-size-fits-all due to diverse use cases and constraints.

today: RFC 7397 is an Informational document summarizing a 2012 workshop. It has not been obsoleted. Follow-up standardization work led to the creation of the LWIG, DICE, and ACE working groups within the IETF.

sections.title: Overview of Smart Object Security
sections.content:
Smart objects (Internet of Things devices) are small, resource-constrained devices being deployed at scale in homes, buildings, and industries. Unlike traditional computers, they have limited memory, battery life, and processing power, yet still need security.

A workshop held in Paris on March 23, 2012, brought together security researchers and implementers to discuss how existing IETF security protocols could be applied to smart objects. The workshop aimed to understand what has been deployed, what works, and what gaps remain.
sections.eli5: Tiny connected devices need protection from bad actors, but they cannot handle the full security tools that big computers use. Experts got together to figure out simpler ways to protect them.

sections.title: Requirements and Use Cases
sections.content:
Different smart object deployments have very different security needs. A light bulb in a consumer home has different threats and requirements than a smart meter in the power grid or a sensor in an industrial facility.

Key questions include: who are the actors? Who provisions credentials? What constraints apply? What authorization is needed? And what tasks will end users need to perform? The workshop heard from experts working with consumer devices, enterprise systems, and industrial deployments, each facing distinct challenges around usability and security tradeoffs.
sections.eli5: A smart light bulb needs different protection than a power meter or a factory sensor. The experts talked about what each type of device needs to be safe.

sections.title: Implementing Security on Constrained Devices
sections.content:
Participants demonstrated that IETF security protocols—including TLS, DTLS, and public key cryptography—are implementable on very constrained devices, even with limited RAM and CPU. The three main constraints are code size, energy consumption, and bandwidth.

A surprising finding: the energy cost of transmitting data wirelessly far exceeds the cost of expensive cryptographic operations like public key signatures. This means security does not have to sacrifice performance in the way developers might fear. The key is to optimize the entire protocol stack, not just individual algorithms. Existing security protocols can be customized through cipher suite selection, feature elimination, and architectural choices to fit different deployment scenarios.
sections.eli5: Even tiny devices can use strong security. Sending a radio message uses more power than doing hard math, so devices do not slow down much when they use security.

sections.title: Authorization and Access Control
sections.content:
Authorization—deciding who gets to access what—differs from authentication. Smart object deployments use two main approaches: access control lists matching authenticated identifiers, or attribute-based schemes using roles and properties.

Systems may delegate authorization decisions to a trusted server, or store policies on the device itself. Different deployment scenarios call for different approaches. The workshop found that existing mechanisms like OAuth, Kerberos, EAP/AAA, and attribute certificates already cover many use cases, and in many deployments, authorization decisions can remain internal to the system without needing new standards.
sections.eli5: Once a device proves who it is, someone has to decide what it is allowed to do. There are many ways to make these decisions, and the right way depends on how the smart objects are used.

sections.title: Getting Credentials into Devices
sections.content:
When a smart object enters a network, it needs to be provisioned with security credentials. This can happen before shipment, at installation, or during an initial 'phone home' to the manufacturer.

For consumer devices, pairing with out-of-band verification (showing matching numbers on two devices, for instance) works for small numbers of devices. For large deployments, having devices contact a central provisioning server is common. Important questions include: what happens if the manufacturer goes out of business? How are credentials transferred when devices are resold? How can the compromise of a manufacturer's key be prevented from affecting already-deployed devices?
sections.eli5: When a new device is plugged in, it needs to learn secret keys so it can talk safely to other devices. People have different ways of giving devices these secrets depending on how many devices there are and who is setting them up.
